A Plan Before the Next Hard Day

Mama was humming over a cup of tea. The spoon lay on the saucer, and her thumb kept time against the handle. I knew the hymn. She’d played it at church for years, back when she could tell you which soprano had come in early and exactly how early she’d come in.

By then, Dot couldn’t give me a full sentence. The tune came through anyway.

I sat down instead of picking up the cup.

That moment belongs later in our story, not to the day of her diagnosis. Dot was a person I loved, with a sharp ear and opinions about nearly everything. A care plan was supposed to serve her.

The tea had gone pale. I had been standing with one hand ready to take away the saucer, already thinking about the next thing waiting for me. Sitting put my ears closer to the little tune. She reached the part I remembered, then went back over it. I didn’t need to find a lesson in every note.

There was still work waiting when I got up. Sitting hadn’t canceled it. But I wanted arrangements that left room for being her daughter, not just the person who arrived carrying the next job. That small distinction mattered to me at the table.

You may be reading with an appointment card beside you. Perhaps your parent has a diagnosis. Perhaps you’re still waiting for an explanation and don’t know what to call the changes you’ve seen. You can want answers and dread getting them at the same time.

You don’t have to settle that feeling before doing the next useful thing.

The job nobody handed over

There may be no clear moment when you become the lead caregiver. A call comes to you because you answered the last one. You agree to make an appointment. Someone asks you to keep the details, since you already have them. Before long, the word “we” in a family conversation seems to mean you.

Consider how a small favor can grow. You offer to find an office’s opening hours. Now you have the number, so someone asks you to make the call. When the office hasn’t replied, everyone asks you for news. The original favor took a minute; the waiting and explaining have no end marked on them. Nobody has asked whether you can keep doing that part.

Being nearby can put you in that position. So can having a flexible lunch break, or simply being willing to answer. None of those things tells the family how much time you actually have. A lunch break is not an empty afternoon.

I would separate the favor you accepted from the continuing job people have attached to it. You can agree to get an answer this time and still say that someone else must handle the next request. That is a change in the work, not a withdrawal of affection.

If that sounds familiar, I have an objection to the advice that you should take everything one day at a time. Some days, yes. But an appointment needs making before the morning you need to attend it. Help needs asking for while you still have enough attention to explain the job.

I spent years dispatching trucks for a freight company. A driver with a flat needed to know who was coming and what happened to the delivery. When I began helping care for Mama, I wanted that same certainty.

I couldn’t have it. I could give a job a name, though, and stop relying on everybody remembering the same conversation.

I’ll tell you what helped: making a few arrangements while the day was still ordinary. That is what I mean by building systems. Not buying an app. Not making your kitchen look like an office. An arrangement that somebody else can understand without you standing beside them is enough.

One arrangement might concern family updates. Suppose you’ve answered the same question in three separate messages and then been asked why you didn’t tell a fourth relative. You could agree that ordinary updates will go in one family message thread after the person handling a task reports back. “The office called; the appointment is confirmed for Tuesday” belongs there once. Urgent concerns still need direct contact with someone who can respond; a message thread isn’t emergency help.

Another arrangement might make an offer usable. “I can help on Friday” leaves you guessing whether that means a whole day or twenty minutes. “I can handle the return call between nine and eleven, but I’m at work after that” gives you something definite. You might not like the limit. At least you won’t build Friday around help that disappears at lunchtime. No one should have to disclose their whole private life to explain that they aren’t available.

A third might settle what happens when an answer hasn’t arrived. Someone has called, left a message, and heard nothing. That isn’t the same as forgetting the job. Agreeing that they will report the unanswered call on Wednesday lets you distinguish waiting from work nobody accepted. It also gives you a chance to decide who follows up, rather than silently taking it back yourself.

These are examples of agreements, not a new filing system to maintain. Choose one that removes an actual piece of guessing from your day.

I want the first year to be about getting those arrangements in place before you’re trying to invent them during a hard afternoon. That doesn’t mean a plan can prevent every crisis. It means you shouldn’t also have to remember who agreed to return a phone call.

You may already be well past the diagnosis visit. Start where you are.

An owner, a drop date, and no guilt in the driver’s seat

My first rule is that every task gets an owner and a drop date. Dispatch language. A drop date is the agreed day the job will be done, or the day its owner reports back if it can’t be done yet.

“We should ask about that” is a wish. “I’ll call the office Tuesday and tell you what they say” is a job somebody has accepted. If the office can’t answer, the next step still needs a person attached to it.

The owner doesn’t have to be you. Nor does the person doing a job have to do it my way. I care whether the call gets made, not whether somebody uses my favorite pen.

Being the contact person is different from being the person who does everything. If your family has handed you both roles without discussing either, you are allowed to ask for a different arrangement.

My second rule is that guilt is not a planning tool.

It can tell you that you should have noticed earlier. It will happily occupy the whole evening without making a single phone call.

That’s guilt. Set it down.

I don’t mean you’ll stop feeling it because I said so. I mean it doesn’t get to decide who is available on Thursday. Your health and the actual help available belong in that decision. A plan that requires you to be available without interruption isn’t one I’m going to recommend.

You can love your parent and say that an arrangement isn’t workable. You can be disappointed with the options and still choose the best one you can actually carry out. I won’t ask you to feel cheerful about it.

Read for the week you’re in

The chapter numbers below begin at 10. Use the labels as printed; Chapter 15a is the daily-care chapter, not a page you’ve missed.

This week, read Chapters 10, 11, 13 and 14. This month, handle Chapters 15a, 16, 17 and 18. Return to Chapters 12, 15 and 19 as communication, behavior and care needs change.

The first group starts with understanding the diagnosis and preparing for doctor visits, then turns to home safety and driving. The next group makes room for daily care, early legal and financial questions, paying for care, and your own health. The chapters you’ll revisit concern communication, difficult behaviors, and considering memory care.

That’s a reading route, not a requirement to wait. An immediate health or safety concern takes precedence over finishing a chapter. Seek appropriate professional or emergency help rather than reading on to see whether your situation appears in an example.

If a conversation is going badly today, go to Chapter 12 today. If you need to consider memory care now, Chapter 19 is there now. Reading ahead isn’t a prediction about your parent. You can gather information without making a decision that afternoon.

You also don’t owe this book an uninterrupted weekend. I would rather you use one page than finish the book and feel you have acquired another set of obligations.

An interruption doesn’t mean you have to begin again at the first page. Suppose work called you away for several days, and you come back to the book with a different appointment date and an unanswered question. The old bookmark tells you where you stopped reading. It doesn’t tell you what matters now.

Take the question that’s still live and go to its chapter. If a clinician or another professional has given you instructions, follow those rather than substituting the book’s reading order. Then return to the week or month group for anything still unresolved. Reading a chapter and settling the matter it raises are different things. You may need another conversation before an answer is useful.

You can also leave a chapter alone when it isn’t needed today. Put a brief note beside its title about what would bring you back: a question you couldn’t answer, for instance, or a decision your family has begun discussing. That’s a place to resume, not a prediction of decline.

The route can be revised without declaring the whole plan a failure. Keep an arrangement that still works. Change the one that no longer fits the help available. A missed reading week doesn’t erase a call somebody already made.

What these pages can do

This is a book about the work around caring for a parent with dementia. It offers ways to prepare a question, share a task, and notice what you need help answering. It isn’t medical, legal or financial advice.

For questions about symptoms or treatment, contact your parent’s treating clinician: an answer needs their health history, not a resemblance to a story here. Don’t start, stop or change medicines because of something you read in this book. Questions about legal authority or documents belong with a licensed elder law attorney; rules differ by state, so ask how yours applies. For a financial decision specific to your family, get qualified advice before acting.

Where a chapter discusses a health fact or a coverage rule, it names the source so you can check the current information. The National Institute on Aging, Medicare.gov and the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services are among those sources. Local services and program rules can change. A paragraph printed here can’t confirm what is available to your parent today.

For general downsizing and moving logistics, the companion book Downsizing a Parent covers that ground.

Margaret “Maggie” Holloway is a pen name, and the personal stories here are composites written to illustrate real situations, not accounts of identifiable families. I claim no professional credential. The stories aren’t evidence that a choice will suit your parent.

For tonight, open Chapter 10. Read until you find one question you need answered, then write it down in your own words. Leave room underneath for the answer.

Chapter 10: Understanding the Diagnosis

The appointment is over, but the daughter hasn’t put her pen away. In this imagined diagnosis-day conversation, her father sits beside her, holding the folded sheet the office gave him. She has written “dementia” near the top of her notebook. Below it she has written “Alzheimer’s?” with a question mark.

He looks at the page. “Which one did they say I have?”

She isn’t sure whether those words mean the same thing. She heard the explanation. She also heard the word she had been dreading, and the rest became harder to hold on to.

The useful next move is to ask the office to clarify what the clinician concluded. Not to choose a diagnosis from a search result while sitting in the parking lot.

If you’re in that parking lot, leave your notebook open. This week’s job is to understand what has been diagnosed, what remains uncertain, and what the clinician wants to happen next. You don’t have to turn yourself into a person who can read a brain scan.

What the word dementia does and doesn’t tell you

The National Institute on Aging, part of the National Institutes of Health, describes dementia as a decline in thinking abilities serious enough to interfere with everyday life. Remembering is part of it. So are reasoning and understanding. Its dementia overview makes another point plainly: dementia is not a normal part of aging.

That matters when someone dismisses a concern with “Well, he’s getting older.” Growing older doesn’t by itself explain a loss of ability that needs medical attention. On the other hand, one forgotten name doesn’t establish dementia either. You need an assessment, not a family vote between “nothing’s wrong” and the worst thing anyone can imagine.

Dementia describes a set of difficulties. It doesn’t name one disease. Alzheimer’s disease is one cause; other causes can produce overlapping difficulties. Think of “dementia” as the broad description and the type as information about what is causing it. You can ask for both in ordinary language.

According to NIA, symptoms can involve trouble expressing thoughts, changes in judgment or personality, and problems with movement, as well as memory loss. A parent who remembers an old address may still have difficulties elsewhere, and trouble finding words needs evaluation even if the family hasn’t noticed much forgetting.

Your parent’s preferences still belong in a conversation about care. I would keep the person in the conversation rather than let the paperwork become the only voice in the room.

If you haven’t received a diagnosis, contact the primary care office about the changes you’re seeing. Don’t use the descriptions below to decide which disease your parent has. Their purpose is to make the words less strange when a clinician uses them.

The type gives you a better question

NIA’s overview names Alzheimer’s disease, vascular dementia, Lewy body dementia, frontotemporal dementia and mixed dementia among the types. These aren’t five separate boxes into which a family can sort symptoms at home. The overlap is one reason an accurate diagnosis can take careful work.

Alzheimer’s disease

NIA identifies Alzheimer’s as the most common form of dementia and describes brain changes involving proteins called amyloid and tau. In its Alzheimer’s explanation, NIA says memory problems can be an early sign, but difficulties with words, reasoning or judging what is seen can also appear early.

Ask the clinician which abilities are affected in your parent and how that fits the diagnosis. Remembering something well doesn’t settle whether the disease is present.

Vascular dementia

“Vascular” refers to blood vessels. NIA explains that vascular dementia results from conditions that damage vessels in the brain or interfere with the brain’s blood and oxygen supply. Its vascular dementia page describes possible difficulties with familiar tasks, following instructions and language, among other changes.

NIA also notes that not everyone who has a stroke develops dementia. So a stroke history is something for the doctor to assess, not a diagnosis the family can make. Ask what evidence points to a vascular cause in your parent’s case and what existing health conditions the medical team needs to address. Don’t infer a treatment plan from the word “vascular.”

Lewy body dementia

Lewy bodies are abnormal deposits of a protein called alpha-synuclein. NIA’s Lewy body dementia guide describes possible changes in alertness and attention, visual hallucinations, movement difficulties and sleep problems. It also says memory problems may not be apparent at first.

Looking only for forgetting could leave another concern unreported. Seeing something others don’t see doesn’t prove Lewy body dementia. Describe what happened to the clinician and ask whether the team needs further specialist input.

Frontotemporal dementia

Frontotemporal disorders involve damage in the frontal and temporal parts of the brain. The National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke, another NIH institute, explains in its frontotemporal disorders guide that early difficulties can center on behavior, personality or language. Memory may not be the first obvious problem.

If those are the words in your parent’s report, ask which form the clinician suspects and what that means for support now. The family shouldn’t have to force the description into a memory-loss pattern before taking it seriously. A new language difficulty or a marked personality change deserves a medical explanation, not an argument about whether the person is trying hard enough.

Mixed dementia

NIA describes mixed dementia as more than one type occurring together. For example, a person can have Alzheimer’s-related changes alongside vascular changes. “Mixed” doesn’t mean that the office has combined several relatives’ guesses. It describes possible coexisting causes.

Ask which causes the clinician thinks are involved, and how certain they are. There may be more evidence for one component than another. An honest explanation of that uncertainty is more useful than a family-made label that sounds definite but has no medical assessment behind it.

When you write down the suspected type, keep the clinician’s words about confidence beside it. “Likely” and “confirmed” aren’t interchangeable in your notes. If a term isn’t clear, ask what it means in this report rather than supply your own meaning.

How the clinician puts the pieces together

According to NIA’s diagnostic overview, an assessment begins by looking for underlying, potentially treatable conditions that could be contributing to difficulties with thinking. Medical and family history help, along with an examination and appropriate tests. Questions about when changes began are part of that work.

The same overview names medication side effects, vitamin deficiencies and thyroid problems among conditions that can cause serious memory problems resembling dementia. Mood conditions can also contribute to symptoms. These possibilities need clinical evaluation. Finding something treatable is not the same as proving that an established dementia has gone away.

I would resist both easy answers: “There’s nothing to do” and “This one thing will fix everything.” Ask what has been checked. A family member’s guess isn’t enough reason to change what your parent takes.

NIA describes cognitive tests that assess abilities such as memory, problem solving and language, while neurological testing can assess physical functions, including balance and reflexes. The tasks may seem small from the chair beside your parent. Their meaning belongs with the professional evaluating the whole picture.

If a result includes a score, ask what it contributes to the assessment and what else the clinician considered, rather than treating the number as a forecast for next Christmas.

Brain imaging may also be part of the evaluation. NIA describes CT, MRI and PET scans as tools for looking at brain structure, activity or particular changes, depending on the scan. Imaging can help identify problems such as strokes or tumors. These scans do different jobs; a family shouldn’t assume that the newest-sounding one is automatically the right one.

Other selected tests may involve blood or the fluid surrounding the brain and spinal cord. NIA’s overview cautions that blood test results alone shouldn’t be used to diagnose dementia. Ask what a proposed test is intended to answer in your parent’s evaluation. Testing options and availability change, so confirm the current choices with the clinical team rather than use this book as a shopping list.

Not every procedure named on an information page belongs in every person’s assessment. Ask whether a proposed test’s result would change the recommendation. You aren’t expected to order the workup yourself.

Primary care can be the starting point. NIA says the primary care doctor can help find a specialist, and names neurologists, geriatric psychiatrists, neuropsychologists and geriatricians among professionals who may diagnose dementia. A neurologist specializes in the brain and nervous system. A geriatrician focuses on older adults’ health. The other specialists bring expertise in mental health or the assessment of thinking abilities.

Those titles aren’t a ladder you have to climb in order. Ask the referring office which professional is suited to the question that remains. Chapter 11’s written-observation page will help you prepare for that person’s visit; you don’t need to build it here.

Another opinion can have a specific purpose

You can respect a doctor and still ask for a specialist’s assessment or another opinion. I don’t regard that as disloyalty. The question is whether another assessment would help answer something important, not whether you have thanked the first doctor enough or waited a polite length of time to ask again.

NIA notes that similarities among dementia symptoms can make an accurate diagnosis difficult. That is a good reason to ask how confident the clinician is about the type. You might need clarification because the report names only dementia, because proposed testing hasn’t been completed, or because an important change hasn’t been explained.

Be specific about what you want reviewed. “Can another clinician help clarify the likely cause?” is more workable than “We want somebody to tell us everything will be fine.” Another opinion may support the first one. It may leave uncertainty. It isn’t a promise of better news.

Ask the office how to arrange the referral and share the existing results. If there’s no appropriate specialist nearby, NIA suggests contacting the neurology department of the nearest medical school for referral help; a medical school hospital may have a dementia clinic. You can ask about that route without assuming a particular clinic will accept your parent or have an immediate opening.

While another appointment is being arranged, ask the current clinician what to do about unresolved health concerns and what follow-up is needed. Waiting for a specialist should not become an unattended stretch in which nobody knows who is answering a current medical question. Give the referral its owner and drop date from the introduction, but leave the clinical decisions with the medical team.

A stage is a description, not a date

The Alzheimer’s Association’s stages guide uses mild, moderate and severe, also called early, middle and late. It explicitly says these stages are general guides and can overlap. Its descriptions concern Alzheimer’s disease; they are not a universal timetable for every cause of dementia.

In mild or early Alzheimer’s, the Association describes people who may still function independently while having difficulties such as memory lapses or trouble planning. “Mild” is the stage label. It doesn’t mean the diagnosis feels mild to you, or that an individual activity has been cleared as safe.

In moderate or middle Alzheimer’s, difficulties become more pronounced and more assistance is needed. The Association describes trouble expressing thoughts and doing routine tasks without help. In severe or late Alzheimer’s, it describes extensive care needs and major difficulties with communication and physical abilities.

Read those descriptions as an explanation of language you may hear, not a set of scenes you must rehearse tonight. You can ask what support is needed now without imagining every later possibility in detail. When a clinician uses a stage word, ask them to connect it to your parent’s actual abilities.

Progression speed and the course of symptoms vary by person and by dementia type. The Alzheimer’s Association says the rate of Alzheimer’s progression varies; NIA’s Lewy body guide also describes wide individual variation. Neither description gives you a calendar prediction for your parent. The date of diagnosis doesn’t tell you how much assistance will be needed a year from that date.

I would be careful with advice that attaches a care decision to a stage word alone. Ask about the actual task and risk. The home-safety and driving questions in Chapters 13 and 14 need individual attention; “early stage” isn’t permission to set them aside.

There is also an urgent limit to stage language. NIA distinguishes delirium, a sudden state of confusion, from the ongoing problems being assessed for dementia. MedlinePlus, the National Library of Medicine’s health information service, says in its confusion guidance reviewed in 2026 to call 911 or the local emergency number for confusion that begins suddenly. Don’t rename a sudden change “the next stage” and wait for an ordinary appointment.

The CDC’s stroke signs guidance, updated in 2026, gives the emergency rule. Call 911 for sudden confusion, new trouble speaking or understanding, one-sided weakness, sudden vision changes, or other possible stroke signs; note when symptoms began. For other changes that are not emergencies, contact the treating clinician. Their knowledge of your parent’s history matters here. Chapter 15 addresses behavior changes in more detail; a book’s explanation must never replace help for a current health concern.

Your diagnosis-visit question page

Use one sheet for the questions you need answered about this diagnosis. You can take it to the appointment or use it when asking the office for clarification afterward. Put your parent’s name and the visit date at the top. Leave room for answers, rather than squeezing the questions between old notes.

This is a conversation aid, not a diagnostic checklist. Include your parent’s own question if they want one asked. Mark the unanswered question that matters most to you, so an unfinished page still tells you what to pursue next.

  • What is the diagnosis, in plain words, and what exact name should we use?
  • Which dementia type or types do you suspect, and how certain are you?
  • What findings support that conclusion, and what other causes or contributors have you considered?
  • Is anything still being evaluated? What question would another test answer?
  • Would a specialist assessment or second opinion help, and what should it clarify?
  • If you use a stage label, what does it mean for the help my parent needs now?
  • What medical options should we discuss for this diagnosis, and where can we read reliable information about them?
  • Which changes require urgent help? Who handles other questions, and what is the follow-up plan?

Keep answers separate from guesses. If the clinician says the type remains uncertain, write that. For a pending test, record who will explain its result rather than filling the empty space with a confident sentence borrowed from another family’s experience.

You don’t have to get through every question in one sitting. Start with what’s unresolved. An appointment on the calendar and an answer to a pending question are not necessarily the same thing.

Treatment recommendations belong with the clinician who knows your parent’s circumstances. This question page doesn’t recommend a medicine, supplement or treatment change.

Keep the written page where you’ll find it for the next conversation, not buried under the appointment card. Tonight, underline the question that still needs an answer. If you can’t answer the father’s question from the opening — which diagnosis did they give? — contact the office and ask for that clarification first. Leave the pen beside the page.

Chapter 11: Getting the Most From Doctor Visits

Mama had folded her coat across her knees. When the doctor asked how she was doing, Dot said, “Doing fine.” I sat beside her with a notebook still in my pocket. There were things I had meant to mention about the nights at home. I couldn’t find a way to begin without sounding as though I had come to correct her.

The visit lasted ten minutes. We left with the things I needed help with still unsaid.

In the car, I was angry with the visit. Later I had to admit that the doctor couldn’t read the page I hadn’t shown. Mama had answered the question she’d been asked. My notebook hadn’t left my pocket.

I’ll tell you what helped: sending a short written account before the next appointment, then bringing a copy. No speech required. The observations could reach the person who could assess them even if my nerves got the better of me again.

This week’s job is to prepare that account and a current health summary. One describes changes since the last conversation. The other gives a new provider basic health information without requiring you to reconstruct it across a desk.

Get the concern into the room before you do

Ten minutes is a poor container for everything a family has been carrying. A polite opening, an examination and a closing question can leave something important outside the conversation, without anyone being careless.

I wouldn’t make your parent’s answer the obstacle. “Fine” might mean that nothing hurts just then, or that they would rather be somewhere else. Their account and yours can both be heard.

The National Institute on Aging’s appointment-preparation guide recommends writing down concerns, putting them in order and raising the most important ones first, rather than saving the matter that brought you there for the hand already on the door handle.

Choose a main question. “We need help deciding what to do about the change in her sleep” gives your notes a purpose. “We need to talk about everything” doesn’t. Mention other concerns too, and let the clinician determine the clinical priorities.

Before sending health details, ask the office how it accepts a family member’s observations. It may have a patient portal, a form or another approved route. Ask whose attention to mark the note for and when it should arrive. Don’t assume every office needs the same advance notice.

Use the access arrangement the office approves, not your parent’s password borrowed without permission. Ask separately what is needed for the office to discuss care with you. Delivering a note doesn’t settle that question. The legal-authority questions belong in Chapter 16; here, you need to know how this office handles communication.

Nor would I promise your parent that a note is secret; ask the office how it will be used and who may see it. If discussing a particular concern in front of your parent feels difficult or unsafe, tell the staff that and ask how to raise it appropriately. Don’t improvise a private channel and assume it stays private.

If electronic access isn’t workable, ask about a paper route. Keep a dated copy. At the appointment, ask whether the clinician has received the note, and offer your copy if needed rather than relying on a message you can’t confirm was read.

Record changes, not a verdict

Between appointments, keep brief dated notes about changes you need help understanding. Give the clinician something more precise than “She’s worse.” You aren’t conducting a home medical assessment or watching every ordinary afternoon as though it were an examination.

Before any tracking, keep the emergency boundary from Chapter 10. The CDC’s stroke guidance, updated in 2026, directs immediate 911 for sudden confusion, sudden problems producing or understanding speech, abrupt vision changes, weakness on one side, sudden loss of balance, or a sudden severe unexplained headache. Note when the symptoms began, but don’t delay the call to finish a record. MedlinePlus’s confusion guidance reviewed in 2026 also directs emergency help for confusion beginning suddenly. Don’t wait for appointment day.

For changes that aren’t emergencies, contact the treating clinician about when assessment is needed; don’t assume they can wait until the next scheduled visit. Ask what to report sooner and which number to use outside office hours. The clinician needs your parent’s history to judge the concern. These notes can’t make that judgment for you.

Start with sleep. Write what you actually know: when you noticed your parent awake, what they were doing, and whether you were there to observe the rest of the night. “Awake when I checked at midnight” doesn’t establish that they never slept; if you weren’t staying overnight, say so instead of filling the gap with a guess.

NIA’s preparation guide asks patients to report sleep changes, along with changes in appetite, weight and energy. If the clinician wants a particular kind of record, ask them to show you what would be useful.

For a fall, record when and where it happened and what you saw, keeping your account separate from your parent’s if they told you about a fall you didn’t witness. Record any medical help already sought and the instructions received. Don’t turn an unwitnessed fall into a confident explanation about a rug, a shoe or the dementia itself. If your parent is hurt or cannot get up after a fall, call 911 for help. After a blow to the head, worsening headache, repeated vomiting, new confusion, unusual drowsiness, slurred speech or weakness needs immediate emergency care; don’t wait to finish a note or for the appointment. If you suspect a concussion without those signs, contact a health care provider promptly. Tell the treating clinician about every fall, even when no injury is apparent.

These boundaries come from NIA’s falls guide and the CDC’s head-injury danger signs and concussion guidance. Let the treating clinician determine the evaluation needed, especially when a head injury or blood-thinning medicines are involved; don’t try to diagnose the injury at home.

For confusion that has changed gradually, describe the task that became harder and when you first noticed. “Needed help finding the bathroom at home” says more than “Memory bad.” The clinician can assess the meaning; you aren’t assigning a stage. Use the diagnosis questions from Chapter 10 if needed; Chapter 15 addresses behavior patterns.

Be honest about how often something happened. “I saw it once” is usable. Once is enough to report. “Every day” should mean that you have evidence for every day, not that the incident stayed in your mind all week. If another person told you about it, name that source in the note to the clinician.

Put medication changes alongside the observations, with dates when known. Copy the actual name and directions; “the little white one” won’t identify what the prescriber changed. Write who ordered the change and whether you know when your parent started following it. A prescription date and the date the medicine was first taken needn’t be the same.

A sleep change after a new prescription is a reason to ask the prescriber, not evidence that you have found the explanation just because one event followed the other. NIA’s medicine-safety guide advises reporting suspected medicine problems promptly and discussing them with a provider before stopping a medicine. Leave medication decisions with the prescriber; ask a pharmacist when you need help identifying a medicine or understanding its instructions.

Don’t make up missed-dose instructions, and don’t change a dose to test your theory. Ask the prescriber or pharmacist what to do. In a possible emergency, use emergency help rather than waiting for an ordinary medicine question to be answered.

Keep raw notes short enough to continue on a busy day. For the visit, select the observations relevant to the main concern. Provide the whole record if requested, but don’t hide the question under weeks of detail.

Give the next provider a current starting point

A visit note expires as its question gets answered. A health summary travels. Start with one page, dated at the top, and attach a clearly labeled medicine list if it won’t fit legibly, rather than leave out a medicine to meet a page limit.

Include your parent’s name, date of birth, the diagnosis as the clinician recorded it, other known health conditions and relevant operations or hospital visits. Preserve the confidence language from Chapter 10 for an uncertain diagnosis.

Add allergies and known medication reactions as recorded by the health team, along with the names and numbers of the current clinicians and pharmacy. Unknown? Mark it for checking. Guessing an allergy history to fill a blank is worse than leaving a visible question for the office to resolve.

NIA’s medicine-safety guide recommends listing prescriptions, over-the-counter products, vitamins and supplements, including the amount and times taken. For prescriptions, include the prescriber and reason for use. Include occasional products too, not just the bottles lined up beside breakfast. Tell the clinician when the reason for a medicine isn’t known.

Compare the list with the containers and the latest instructions from the medical team. If they disagree, flag the discrepancy and ask the prescriber or pharmacist to resolve it; don’t choose which instruction wins yourself. Mark uncertainty about what was actually taken rather than presenting the label as proof that every dose was taken.

Add how your parent manages ordinary tasks now: what they do independently and what help they receive. Note hearing or vision difficulties. “Daughter helps communicate questions” describes assistance without declaring that your parent has nothing to say.

Put the agreed family contact and their phone number on the page, subject to the office’s communication arrangements, and keep this health information out of public calendars or casual group messages. The appointment card can say where and when; it doesn’t need the medicine list beneath it.

NIA’s appointment guide recommends bringing insurance cards, other doctors’ contact information and medical records the new doctor doesn’t already have. Ask which records the office needs and how to arrange their transfer. Your page can help orient a new provider; it cannot replace the underlying reports or their review.

Update the summary after a verified change. Date it and replace the copy in the appointment folder. Agree who updates it; you don’t need several competing lists maintained with equal enthusiasm.

Leave your parent a place in the conversation

Before the visit, ask what your parent wants to raise. Put that concern on the page too. You may be attending because you can remember details and follow up, but it is still their appointment. NIA’s preparation guide cautions companions against taking too strong a role and notes that patients may want time alone with the doctor.

Tell the staff what help your parent needs to participate. Bring their glasses and working hearing aids if used, as NIA recommends. Ask ahead for an interpreter when needed. These are practical arrangements for the visit, not a test of how well your parent can manage without them.

Allow space for your parent to answer. Add observations without turning the appointment into a contest over who remembers correctly. “I’d like to add what I noticed at home” is enough. For help with difficult conversations, turn to Chapter 12.

With your parent’s agreement where they can give it, confirm who is authorized to receive health details and share only the current information that person needs for the visit, through an agreed private route. Ask the office about the right arrangement when your parent cannot decide or objects; don’t pass a whole medical page to someone merely because they are attending. Say which unanswered concern matters, and leave room for the reply. Don’t depend on a car conversation to deliver the entire health history to a sibling who hasn’t attended before.

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services explains the distinction between sharing information with involved family and friends and the right to access medical records; being related or attending a visit isn’t blanket access.

At the start, tell the clinician about the main concern and any other items you brought. Ask what can be addressed today and what needs another appointment or a different service. If care costs are the unanswered issue, Chapter 17 covers that ground; this page need only record whom the office suggests contacting.

When an instruction isn’t clear, ask for it again in plain words, then read back what you have written so the clinician can check whether you’ve understood correctly. For a medicine instruction, clarify the exact product and directions rather than settling for “continue as before” when you don’t know what “before” refers to.

You also need to know how an unfinished matter will be answered. For a test, ask who explains the result and when to expect contact. Ask what to do if that time passes without an answer. For follow-up, write the proposed timing and who arranges it. A result appearing online doesn’t by itself answer your question about what happens next.

The before-the-visit observation page

Use the following headings on a sheet of paper or in the office’s approved message format. This is the change-focused note, not the health summary or Chapter 10’s diagnosis question page. Write only what you know, leaving uncertainties visible. Keep the completed note to a readable page where possible, with further details available if requested.

  • Parent and appointment: Name, date of birth, visit date and clinician. Your name, relationship and contact details; date of this note.
  • Main concern: The change you want assessed and the question you need answered. Add your parent’s concern in their own words where possible.
  • Before this change: A brief description of the relevant task or sleep pattern before things changed. State what you personally knew.
  • Observed changes: Dated examples involving sleep, falls or gradually changed confusion, as relevant. Say what happened, who observed it and what isn’t known.
  • Medicines or other recent care: Verified prescription changes and start dates, new nonprescription products, emergency visits or other care. Attach the current medicine list rather than guessing names.
  • Help already sought: Whom you contacted, when, the advice received and any question still awaiting an answer.
  • What we need from this visit: The main question, any other concerns to flag, and a request for the next step and follow-up contact.

This form isn’t for storing a sudden change until appointment day. Use the emergency boundary above and the clinician’s reporting instructions before completing paperwork.

After the appointment, add the clinician’s answer and the agreed next step beneath the question, keeping their recommendation separate from your own interpretation so another person can see what was actually advised. If you couldn’t get an answer, write that too, along with whom you will contact and when. Apply the owner and drop date from the introduction to that follow-up, not to a medical decision the family can’t make.

For the next visit, open a fresh page. Carry forward an unresolved question, not every paragraph from the old one. Mama’s “doing fine” wasn’t a reason for me to have nothing ready. Put your parent’s name at the top tonight, write the change you need help understanding, and leave enough white space for someone to answer.

Chapter 12: Talking With Someone Who Is Confused

Seven in the morning, and the same question for the fourth time.

Here is a made-up kitchen, a son and his mother. “What time is the doctor coming?” The appointment is Thursday at ten. He tells her Thursday at ten. She nods, stirs her coffee, looks out at the carport, and eleven minutes later asks what time the doctor is coming.

By the fourth asking his voice has changed. He doesn’t yell. He just lands on the word told. “Mama, I’ve told you three times.”

She goes quiet after that. Not because the answer finally stuck. Because she heard how he said it.

That’s the part that gets missed. The information drops away first; the tone stays in the room a good while longer. You can be right about Thursday and still lose the morning.

This chapter is about the ordinary talking: answering, asking, explaining, getting through a task together. Accusations and suspicion are a different animal, and they wait for Chapter 15.

Correcting costs more than it buys

My instinct, early on, was to fix every wrong detail. The wrong day, the wrong grandchild’s name, the wrong year for a trip. I believed I was being helpful, and some part of me believed that if I kept the facts straight out loud, the facts would stay straight in her head.

They didn’t. What I got instead was a woman who stopped offering sentences, because every sentence had turned into a quiz she kept failing.

I’ll tell you what helped. I let most of it go.

The Alzheimer’s Association’s guidance on memory loss and confusion suggests staying calm, responding with a brief explanation rather than a long one, and offering corrections as suggestions instead of explanations that sound like scolding. Its example is small and useful: “I thought it was a fork.” The Association also notes that in a conversation anchored in another time of life, you can travel there with the person and talk about what they recall, treating it as their current reality. And it says plainly that being called the wrong name, or not being recognized, is not something to take personally, however much it stings.

Its communication guidance puts the same idea in two lines worth keeping on a card: avoid criticizing and correcting; avoid arguing, and if the person says something you don’t agree with, let it be.

That’s the opposite of advice families often get, which is to reorient the person to today’s date and today’s facts every single time. I’d be careful with that one. Insisting on reality doesn’t restore it, and if the only reliable product of a correction is distress, you’ve bought nothing.

There’s a line I won’t draw for you, because I can’t. What to say when your mother asks for a husband who died in 1998 is the hardest question in this book, and families settle it differently, some with a brief honest answer, some by asking what she remembers about him. Ask your parent’s care team what they’d suggest, and ask your local Alzheimer’s Association chapter; they’ve heard the question from people in your exact spot.

One thing stays fixed whichever way you go. Talk with your parent as an adult, not as a child. The National Library of Medicine’s MedlinePlus guide to dementia daily care, reviewed in April 2026, says that outright: speak to people who have dementia as adults, and don’t pretend to understand them when you don’t. Baby talk is a correction too. It just arrives in a kinder voice.

Set the room before you set the sentence

Half of what goes wrong in these conversations was decided before anybody opened their mouth.

The MedlinePlus daily-care guide recommends cutting distraction and noise first: turn down or turn off the radio or television, close the curtains, move to a quieter room. It suggests making eye contact before you touch or speak to the person, so you’re not arriving out of nowhere.

Then the sentence itself. That same source recommends simple words and short sentences, spoken slowly, in a quiet voice. Volume isn’t the fix. Talking loudly, as though the person were hard of hearing, doesn’t help if hearing isn’t the problem. Repeat your words when you need to. Use the names of people and places your parent knows, and go easy on pronouns, since he, she and they can leave a listener hunting for who’s being discussed. If you change the subject, say that you’re changing it.

Two more, from the Association’s communication guidance: speak directly to the person rather than to whoever brought them, and don’t leave them out of conversations happening in front of them. If a pharmacist asks you how your parent is sleeping while your parent is standing there, you can bring them into the question: ‘Mama, do you want to tell her about the nights?’

The Association also suggests asking what the person is still comfortable doing and where they’d like help, and agreeing on which way of communicating suits them best, whether that’s sitting face to face, a phone call or something written. Ask early; you may need to ask again as your parent’s preferences or abilities change.

And timing counts. A question that goes nowhere at six in the evening may land fine at ten in the morning. If you’ve got something that genuinely needs discussing, take it to the hour of day your parent does best, whatever hour that turns out to be. Why late-day hours run rougher for some people is Chapter 15’s subject, not this one.

Sensory trouble muddies all of it. The Association notes that vision and hearing loss may also be present in someone with dementia, which makes communication harder still. It adds that many such problems can be addressed, with hearing aids or prescription lenses, and recommends having hearing and eyesight checked regularly and asking your parent’s doctor whether either is affecting communication. Before you conclude that your father has lost more words this month, find out whether his hearing aid has a dead battery. Add the hearing and vision question to the summary you built in Chapter 11 and let the clinician sort out what’s what.

One thing at a time, and the time to answer it

Most of us ask stacked questions without noticing. “Do you want to get dressed now or after breakfast, and did you want the blue shirt, and should I run the bath first?” That’s three decisions and a plan, delivered in one breath, to someone who may still be working on the first word.

The Association’s middle-stage communication tips go the other way. One question at a time. Yes-or-no questions where you can: “Would you like some coffee?” rather than “What would you like to drink?” Clear, step-by-step instructions, since a long request can be too much to hold. Visual cues, including showing a task rather than describing it. And written notes, which can land when spoken words don’t.

MedlinePlus adds the same approach from its side: break directions into small, simple steps, allow time for the person to understand, offer clear choices with something to point at, and don’t pile on options. If frustration sets in, it suggests switching to another activity rather than pushing through.

Then the hardest instruction on the list. Wait.

The Association recommends giving the person plenty of time to respond and not interrupting unless help is asked for. A pause that feels endless to you is often just the time a sentence now takes to assemble. Count it out if you have to. Finishing your parent’s sentences is efficient, and it teaches them that talking is something other people do faster.

Keep one thing straight about all these adjustments. They make a conversation work; they don’t measure what your parent can still do. A father who follows a two-step instruction in a quiet kitchen has not thereby been cleared to drive, manage his own medicines or stay alone overnight. Those are clinical and safety judgments, and they belong with his doctor and the chapters that deal with them.

When the same question comes back

Treat a repeated question as a fresh chance to respond, without assuming why it returned. Answer briefly; if the worry remains, ask what feels uncertain.

For the question in the kitchen scene, the uncertainty might be about what happens next, not just the time. The Association, writing about late-stage communication, makes the general point: the feelings behind the words can matter more than the words. You can add a concrete detail to the answer: “Thursday. I’m driving you, and I’ll be here early.”

Written notes earn their place here. A card by the chair that says Dr. Pham, Thursday 10 a.m., John driving gives your parent somewhere to go besides you. Some people check the card a dozen times and settle. Some never look at it. You’ll find out which you’ve got.

Don’t buy quiet with a promise you can’t keep. “We’ll go see the old house tomorrow,” said to end a repeated question, buys you about a day and costs you the next conversation.

Repeated stories are a lighter problem, and I’d treat them lightly. If your mother tells you about the ice storm in Statesville for the third time this week, you’re not obliged to log it as a symptom or to announce that you’ve heard it. Let it run. Ask what the roads were like. You are allowed to simply enjoy your parent.

The Association’s early-stage guidance makes a point about this that I’d underline for every relative who has gone quiet since the diagnosis: don’t assume what someone can or can’t do with a conversation because of a diagnosis, and don’t pull away. It says the disease affects each person differently, and that your honesty, friendship and support still matter. It even says that laughing is allowed, that humor sometimes lifts the mood and makes talking easier. My mother said funnier things in her last few years than she had in the twenty before, and laughing with her was never the problem. Laughing at her would have been.

This is also the thing to tell the grandchildren and the brother-in-law who keeps finding reasons not to visit. They are usually not avoiding your parent. They’re avoiding the fear of saying the wrong thing. Hand them two sentences and a job, something ordinary with a start and a finish, and most of them manage fine.

There is a line where a communication technique stops being the right tool. The Association’s memory-loss guidance says that any sudden change in behavior should get a medical evaluation to rule out other causes, and lists infections, a change in living arrangements and a switch in routine among the things that can make symptoms worse. A parent who was managing conversation last week and can’t today needs a clinician, not a better phrase. New trouble producing or understanding speech that comes on suddenly is an emergency: call 911, as the CDC’s stroke guidance directs, and note what time it started.

Safety also outranks technique. MedlinePlus’s guide to dementia behavior and sleep problems, also reviewed in April 2026, advises against touching or restraining someone during an angry outburst unless safety requires it. It suggests staying calm, trying to distract the person, and not taking the behavior personally. And if you or your parent is in danger, that guide says to call 911 or your local emergency number. Don’t stay in the room trying a better phrase. That instruction comes before every piece of advice in this chapter.

A say-this-not-that card

Copy these onto an index card and leave it where the hard conversations happen, which for most families is the kitchen. They’re swaps, not scripts. Your mother’s name and your father’s history go in them, or they’ll sound like somebody else talking.

  • Instead of “I already told you, it’s Thursday,” try: “Thursday at ten. I’m driving you.”
  • Instead of “Don’t you remember your own granddaughter?”, try: “That’s Julie, your granddaughter. She’s got your eyes.”
  • Instead of “That’s not a fork, it’s a spoon,” try: “I think that’s the spoon. Here’s the fork.”
  • Instead of “Mama, Daddy died years ago,” keep this reminder: “When your parent asks for someone who has died, don’t borrow a stock answer from this card. Acknowledge the feeling, notice how your parent responds, and ask their care team what approach fits this person.”
  • Instead of “Do you want a shower now or later, and which shirt?”, try: “Would you like a shower now?” and ask about the shirt afterward.
  • Instead of “Hurry up, we’re late,” try: “We need to leave soon. Let’s do one thing at a time.” Then say nothing and let the sentence arrive.
  • Instead of “You can’t do that anymore,” try: “Let me get the first part started.” Leave the clinical judgment to the clinician.
  • Instead of “What did you do today?”, try: “Did you sit out on the porch today?”
  • Instead of talking over your parent to another adult, try: “Mama, do you want to tell him, or should I?”

Some swaps will sound natural to your family; others won’t. Keep what helps and revise what doesn’t.

What to try this week

Pick one sentence you keep saying that keeps going badly. Mine was a version of “I just told you.” Write down what you’ll say instead, in your own words, and put it somewhere you’ll see it before your parent is standing in front of you.

The goal isn’t a perfect conversation. Some days the exchange that matters is three words long and mostly about the fact that you sat down.

Chapter 13: Home Safety and Wandering

The screen door catches on its spring. The daughter comes out of the kitchen.

In this imagined near-miss, her father is on the porch in his slippers, one hand on the railing. His coat is still on its hook. He says he needs to get to work. The daughter had stepped away to rinse a plate; she thought he was watching television.

She goes to him. They come back inside together. Nothing terrible has happened, and her hands are shaking anyway.

Later, her brother says they ought to get a better lock.

A door that your father cannot open can keep him inside during a fire, too. You need a way to notice an exit, someone who can respond, and a usable escape route.

This week’s job is a safety pass through the house and a written plan for a missing parent. If your parent is missing now, call 911 and tell the dispatcher they have dementia. Don’t finish reading first.

Walk the route your parent actually uses

Start at your parent’s chair and follow the route to the bathroom. Then walk from the bed. Look at the floor, the light switches, the narrow turn beside the dresser. A tidy-looking house can still have a cord across the path someone uses in the dark.

The Alzheimer’s Association’s home safety guidance recommends removing throw rugs, extension cords and excess clutter from walking routes. It also calls for even lighting between rooms and at stairs and entries, with night lights in bedrooms, bathrooms and halls.

Put the reading lamp’s cord against the wall rather than across the trip to the kitchen, and move the shopping bag waiting beside the chair before you check the route again after dark.

No risky demonstration needed. Check the steps themselves.

Remove the obstacle without making a trial of who left it there.

The Association says a home should support independence and social interaction rather than feel too restrictive. Clear a space at the table without stripping the room of everything your parent enjoys.

The same guidance recommends securing large televisions, cabinets and bookcases against tipping. If you don’t know how to anchor an item properly, get qualified installation help.

In the bathroom, the Association recommends grab bars by the shower, tub and toilet, and nonslip treatment for slippery surfaces. Ask an occupational therapist or home-safety professional which supports fit your parent’s abilities and how they should be installed. Don’t assume a towel rail is a grab bar. The bathing routine itself belongs in Chapter 15a; here, you’re checking the room around it.

The fall-and-head-injury boundary in Chapter 11 still applies. Tell the treating clinician about falls and ask for an individual safety assessment when walking, vision or transfers have become difficult. Changing the room doesn’t replace that assessment.

Before buying anything, name the problem. “Can’t see the step from the hallway” gives you something to ask about. “Need all the dementia safety products” doesn’t.

The kitchen needs more than a reminder

A note saying Turn off the stove may not be enough protection when using the stove has become unsafe. You need to address access to the hazard, not keep making the note larger.

The Association’s home safety page suggests appliances with automatic shutoff and measures to prevent unsafe stove use, including knob covers or removing knobs. Ask a home-safety professional about the appropriate arrangement for the appliance and your parent’s current abilities. Gas or electrical changes belong with a qualified professional; don’t improvise a disconnection because an online list mentions it.

An automatic feature doesn’t settle whether your parent can use the appliance alone, so discuss that question with the care team before treating the gadget as permission to leave. Until then, provide the needed help.

Look at what is sitting beside the kettle. The Association recommends taking medicines and vitamins off counters and tables and storing medication in a locked drawer or cabinet. Arrange safe access for the person responsible for giving it. This is storage, not permission to change a medicine or its directions; keep the prescriber-and-pharmacist boundary from Chapter 11.

In the laundry area, secure cleaning products out of sight in their original containers. The Association specifically warns about laundry packets and bleach. A decorative jar makes a poor place for something that isn’t food. Check the garage and workroom for accessible chemicals or equipment as well. Don’t confine your parent to secure a bottle; secure the bottle.

Put smoke and carbon monoxide alarms on the safety pass. The Association says these devices should be available and inspected regularly. If there are firearms in the house, its guidance recommends removal or locked storage. Ask for qualified help with safe handling or storage rather than handling an unfamiliar firearm yourself. This chapter isn’t a firearm-handling guide.

Notice risk before an actual disappearance

In its wandering guidance, checked in October 2026, the Alzheimer’s Association states that six in ten people living with dementia will wander at least once. This is its currently published estimate, not a newly dated study or an individual prediction.

The Association says wandering can happen at any stage. Use the figure as a reason to prepare, not a reason to watch your parent as though every trip to the porch were wrongdoing.

The warning signs on that page include taking longer than expected on a familiar walk, forgetting a familiar route, pacing, and appearing lost in changed surroundings. A person may talk about an old job or say they need to go home while sitting in their own house. Difficulty finding rooms at home is another sign the Association names.

Those signs give you something to discuss with the care team. They don’t prove that every restless afternoon will end in a disappearance. Nor does the absence of a previous incident make a missing-person plan unnecessary.

After a near-miss, contact the treating clinician promptly about what happened and what supervision is needed now. Don’t wait for a repeat to justify the call. Sudden confusion still takes the emergency route from Chapter 10; don’t file it under wandering and wait for a safety appointment.

A parent can also get lost by car. Once driving has stopped, the Association recommends removing access to car keys. Deciding about driving and arranging that transition belong in Chapter 14. Here, check that an agreed restriction isn’t undone by the spare keys on the hall hook.

The wandering guidance recommends areas that can be explored safely, indoors or outside. Ask the care team how to support that for this person. The aim isn’t to eliminate every enjoyable movement.

An alarm must have someone at the other end

A door alarm tells you a door has opened. It doesn’t bring your parent back.

The Association lists warning bells and door-monitoring devices among measures to consider. Before relying on any door alarm, monitoring device or lock placement, have your parent’s doctor, the local fire department, or an occupational-therapy or home-safety professional review the setup. Explain who is present during the day and overnight, because an arrangement built around an awake companion in the house is different from one depending on a phone notification reaching somebody elsewhere.

Ask who will hear or receive an alert, and who can respond in person. Try the agreed system while your parent is safely accompanied, from the places the caregiver actually occupies. If it uses a phone, check its sound and notification settings. Ask the provider what happens during loss of power, an internet outage or a depleted battery. Write the backup arrangement, rather than assuming the device will announce its own failure.

If nobody can respond promptly, tell the care team that. Don’t substitute a lock or a promise to check the screen more often for missing supervision. If there is immediate danger and you cannot keep your parent safe, call 911 for help.

GPS equipment deserves the same skepticism. The Association’s technology safety guidance says tracking can be inaccurate, may work poorly inside buildings, and should be used alongside other safety measures. It is not a companion. A location dot may help a search; it isn’t proof that a person is safe where the dot appears.

Ask how a device stays with your parent and who keeps it charged. Talk with your parent about monitoring where they can participate, and ask the care team about privacy and consent questions if that is difficult. Don’t quietly turn every room into a recorded space because a camera was easy to order.

The Association’s wandering page also suggests deadbolts above or below the usual line of sight. In the same instruction it says never to lock a person in at home. Read those together. This is not a recommendation to install an unreachable bolt yourself. If a proposed lock prevents your parent from getting out, reject that arrangement and ask for another approach.

Every emergency exit must remain usable by your parent and the caregiver, with assistance arranged where needed; first responders must be able to reach them and use the escape routes. A caregiver’s hidden key is not an escape plan for a parent alone behind a locked door. Neither is an app that has to connect before the door will open.

The U.S. Fire Administration’s home fire escape guidance, checked in 2026, calls for unblocked doors and windows and an outside meeting place. Have the local fire department review how your household would get out, including your parent’s actual need for help, and ask about local requirements before changing door hardware. A dementia label on the package isn’t enough.

I wouldn’t buy a door device before making that call. The question isn’t just whether it keeps someone from leaving. It’s whether everyone can leave when they must.

A room-by-room safety pass

Never lock your parent in. Keep emergency exits usable for your parent, caregivers and first responders. Have any alarm, monitoring device or lock placement reviewed before relying on it.

Walk through with this checklist. Mark an item complete only when the arrangement works; write who will handle anything unfinished. A professional review still pending is an open task, not a checked box.

  • Walking routes: Remove loose rugs, bags and trailing cords; check even lighting from chair and bed to bathroom, at stairs and at entries.
  • Bedroom and sitting room: Check night lighting, accessible needed items and large furniture secured against tipping; seek help for installation or mobility questions.
  • Bathroom: Identify slippery surfaces and needed grab bars; have suitable supports properly assessed and installed without blocking access.
  • Kitchen: Address unsafe stove access with qualified help; check appropriate shutoff features and safe, secured medicine storage without changing treatment directions.
  • Laundry, garage and workroom: Secure cleaning products in original containers; restrict access to hazardous chemicals and equipment, not escape routes.
  • Exterior doors and yard: Arrange reviewed alerts with an actual responder and backup; check all exits remain usable. After driving stops, secure every accessible set of car keys.
  • Fire and other hazards: Check smoke and carbon monoxide alarms; ask the fire department about escape assistance. Arrange qualified help for any firearm safety concern.
  • Caregiver handoff: Show the next caregiver the reviewed setup, needed access and backup arrangements; put the missing-person card somewhere they can find it.

Bring an unhelpful change back to the professional who reviewed it. Recheck after a new safety incident or a change in abilities; a completed pass describes today’s house, not every future need.

When you cannot find your parent

Prepare the information before you need it. The Association recommends keeping a recent close-up photograph, identifying dangerous areas nearby, and listing places your parent might head toward, such as a former workplace or place of worship. Ask trusted neighbors to contact you if they see your parent apparently lost. They are extra eyes, not a replacement for needed care.

Keep the photo available to responders and the card accessible to an agreed caregiver. Don’t post private health details publicly as a precaution. Ask local police through their non-emergency contact about dementia-response services and the information they need. Availability varies; registration doesn’t replace 911.

The Association’s wandering page says to begin searching immediately and call 911 if the person hasn’t been found within fifteen minutes. That instruction is not a required waiting period. For this book’s conservative action card, call 911 as soon as you realize your parent with dementia is missing. Report an unknown departure time as unknown. Tell the dispatcher about immediate hazards, including traffic, water or dangerous weather, and follow their instructions.

Look in the immediate surroundings without delaying the call or putting yourself in danger. If another adult is available, one can speak with the dispatcher while the other checks nearby. Tell responders about the places on your list and any location-device information; don’t treat a tracker as a reason to postpone help. Don’t enter water or another dangerous area yourself.

Give the last confirmed sighting, not the time you wish they had left. “I saw him in the sitting room before I went into the kitchen” is an honest starting point. Distinguish what you saw from what a neighbor reported. Keep your phone available for responders, and tell them immediately if your parent returns.

Your missing-person action card

Write these details on one page now. This is an emergency aid, not another health-summary template.

  1. Call: 911 as soon as the parent with dementia is missing. State the dementia diagnosis, their name and the address or location they disappeared from. Follow dispatcher instructions; don’t wait fifteen minutes.
  2. Last confirmed sighting: Time and place, or clearly marked uncertainty. Current clothing, footwear and any mobility aid, if known.
  3. Identification: Recent close-up photo and an accurate physical description. Contact number for the caregiver speaking with responders.
  4. Nearby risks and possible destinations: Traffic, water or other hazards; former addresses, workplace, place of worship and previous destinations, if relevant.
  5. Search coordination: Who is checking the immediate vicinity, who remains reachable, and any tracking information. Do not delay emergency contact or enter dangerous areas.
  6. When found: Notify responders immediately, follow their instructions and report any injury or sudden confusion. Contact the treating clinician about the incident and review the safety arrangement before using it again.

Nobody has to prove they were a good caregiver before making that call. Give the dispatcher the facts you have. Tonight, take a current photo and put it where the next person helping you can find it without asking.

Chapter 14: The Driving Conversation

Daddy answered the phone, and a deputy asked whether he was Dot’s husband.

Mama had gone for groceries. Coming home, she had lost the route she knew. The deputy called Earl, my father, so someone could come for her.

That detail stayed with me. We had treated familiar roads as protection. They weren’t enough.

In this composite family story, the call made the driving question impossible to put off. I wish we had raised it before somebody had to find Daddy’s number. You don’t need that call to ask for help.

This week’s job is to bring driving to the treating clinician and check your state’s licensing rules. If your parent is already driving against medical advice, address access to the vehicle now, safely, while getting professional help. An appointment weeks away isn’t a safety arrangement for today’s trip.

A familiar road still asks for quick decisions

The National Institute on Aging’s Driving Safety and Alzheimer’s Disease, checked in October 2026, says some people can still drive in early dementia. Worsening memory and decision-making can make driving unsafe. The word early isn’t permission. Your parent’s individual assessment and your state’s rules matter.

Knowing the way to the store doesn’t settle how a driver will respond when a child steps off a curb. NIA says someone with memory loss may manage some driving yet struggle to react quickly to a surprise. The question is today’s decisions, not yesterday’s driving record.

The Alzheimer’s Association’s Driving and Dementia describes difficulty with complex tasks such as driving even at the earliest stages of Alzheimer’s. It recommends planning before driving becomes an issue. A diagnosis visit is a reasonable place to start that conversation, even without a crash.

I wouldn’t begin with how old your parent is. NIA’s safe-driving guidance for older adults recommends discussing driving skills rather than age. A lifetime of being the person everyone trusted behind the wheel deserves respect. It cannot answer a current safety question.

Signs to bring forward, not a score to pass

The Association lists forgotten routes, missed signs, pedal confusion and poor traffic decisions among unsafe-driving warnings; NIA also names new damage and reports from others. Use this checklist to identify a concern, not calculate a cutoff.

  • Getting lost on a familiar route, forgetting the destination, or returning unusually late from a routine errand without a clear explanation.
  • New dents or scrapes, hitting curbs, a near miss, or a crash.
  • Missing stop signs, traffic lights or other road signs; errors at intersections.
  • Confusing the accelerator and brake.
  • Poor lane control, abrupt lane changes, inappropriate speed or slow decisions in traffic.
  • Becoming confused or angry while driving, or receiving a specific report of unsafe driving from someone else.
  • A clinician’s instruction to stop driving, or a failed driving evaluation.

An unexplained dent isn’t a confession. Ask what happened. Get other people’s accounts in their words, separate from what you witnessed, and use the Chapter 11 note route rather than making your parent defend their whole driving history.

Don’t wait for several boxes to be checked. With a warning of unsafe driving, arrange another driver and contact the treating clinician promptly about the event and what assessment is needed. Confusing pedals or missing a signal is not a reason for one more family test drive. Don’t put yourself in the passenger seat to collect proof of a danger you already suspect.

If confusion has begun suddenly, use Chapter 10’s emergency boundary: call 911. Don’t turn a sudden medical change into an ordinary driving appointment.

Ask what the doctor is assessing

Say the question directly: “We need a clinical driving-safety assessment. What should happen about driving now?”

If your mother got lost, say where she meant to go, where she was found and who helped. “Nobody saw the turn she missed” is useful uncertainty. Don’t fill it with a guess.

Ask the clinician to consider the health issues that could affect driving. NIA names vision, hearing and movement problems in its dementia-driving guidance. Its older-driver guidance also explains that medicines can cause drowsiness or reduced alertness. Give the doctor the current medicine information from Chapter 11; don’t stop a prescription to see whether driving improves. Medicine decisions still belong to the prescriber.

An office assessment is not the same thing as a formal on-road driving evaluation. A discussion or test in an examination room doesn’t mean anyone watched your parent respond to traffic. Ask which kind of assessment the office can provide, what its conclusion covers, and whether a separate driving evaluation is appropriate. Don’t assume that a referral slip settles safety while you wait.

The Association recommends a comprehensive evaluation by an occupational-therapy driving rehabilitation specialist for a more objective picture of driving ability than family observation alone. NIA directs families to such specialists, a health professional or their state DMV to find an evaluator, and notes that assessment fees may apply.

When you contact a program, ask whether its service includes a formal on-road component, what happens before that component, and whether your parent’s medical and license status permit it. Some state licensing processes also use road testing; California’s is one example below. An occupational therapist doing a home-safety visit is not automatically the driving specialist you need. Describe the service you’re seeking rather than relying on a job title.

Ask about fees, referral requirements, waiting lists and who receives the report. Confirm coverage with the provider and insurer. When driving is unsafe or restricted, arrange another driver to the evaluation. The appointment doesn’t authorize the journey behind the wheel.

If the clinician advises stopping, don’t wait for a road test to follow that advice. The Association suggests asking the physician to explain the restriction and put it in writing. Clarify the next step and follow-up. If driving is permitted, obtain explicit limits and a reassessment plan consistent with state requirements.

I distrust the family bargain that says “only to the grocery store” without an individual assessment. Mama’s difficulty was on that very errand. Don’t invent a daytime, short-distance exception to a stop-driving recommendation because it sounds easier to enforce.

Say what happened, then say what changes

NIA’s older-driver guidance suggests preparing alternatives before the talk, using “I” statements rather than accusations, and keeping the conversation about safety and continued access to activities. The Association recommends acknowledging the pain of giving up driving while remaining patient and firm.

Use Chapter 12’s communication adjustments away from an imminent departure. Keep your parent involved. Bring an actual offer of help, not a promise that the family will somehow handle everything.

Here is a script to adapt when you’ve observed a concern and are arranging assessment:

“Dad, I’m worried about what happened at the intersection. I want us to ask Dr. Lee about driving. I’m taking you to the appointment, and I’ll drive for now while we get advice. We can still go to the hardware store. Let’s choose when.”

Dr. Lee is a hypothetical name. Use your own observed event and help you can provide. With only a neighbor’s report, say so.

When the clinician has advised stopping, the sentence changes:

“The doctor has said you must not drive. I’m driving today. I know this is upsetting. We can talk about where you want to go.”

Don’t claim a doctor’s order you haven’t received. Don’t say “just for a week” if nobody has promised a review then. Firmness doesn’t require an invented deadline or an invented authority.

Your parent may disagree, and you may have to return to the conversation. The Association cautions that impaired insight and judgment can make the risk hard for the person to recognize. An angry response isn’t evidence that the advice is wrong; a calm response isn’t proof the arrangement will be followed. Check access, not just agreement.

Ask the clinician to join a family conversation if needed. Tell other relatives what was recommended and what ride help is needed.
