A facility search never takes priority over help needed now.

The second is your own health and capacity, the ground Chapter 18 covered in detail. If respite isn’t closing the gap anymore — if you’re exhausted on the good weeks, not just the hard ones — that’s not a personal failing to push through. It’s information.

The third is a mismatch between what your parent now needs and what can realistically happen in a house, even with help. Overnight supervision that no single aide schedule covers. Medical needs that call for more hands, or more trained hands, than you can line up. Behavior changes — discussed in Chapter 15 — that have moved past what tracking and small environmental fixes can manage, where the care team is recommending a different setting, not just a different approach.

None of these signs, alone or together, means you’ve failed at something. They mean the job has changed size. A house can only hold so much supervision before supervision itself becomes the whole day, for one or two people, instead of a staffed team working in shifts.

Sometimes the concern isn’t visible to the relative who visits on Sunday. A missed dose wasn’t noticed when it was due. An attempt to leave was caught only because a neighbor happened to be in the yard. Nobody slept because every sound from down the hall meant getting up to check. Tell the care team what happened and what supervision was available; don’t wait for several incidents to justify asking for help.

After immediate needs are addressed, the dated observations from Chapter 11 can help explain the remaining care gap. Include what you don’t know. An unwitnessed event and a confirmed one aren’t interchangeable, and a quiet afternoon doesn’t establish that overnight supervision is adequate. Ask what must change now while the longer-term options are being assessed.

What “memory care” actually means

The phrase gets used loosely, so it helps to know what it’s standing in for. According to the National Institute on Aging’s Finding Long-Term Care guidance, checked in October 2026, facility-based long-term care includes assisted living, group homes and nursing homes. The differences matter more than the label on the brochure.

Assisted living facilities help with daily tasks — bathing, dressing, medications, meals — but don’t provide around-the-clock medical care. Some have a specific Alzheimer’s or dementia unit, often called “memory care,” with added staffing, structured activities and a secured layout designed around wandering risk. Not every assisted living facility has one, so don’t assume the general label covers dementia-specific support; ask directly.

Group homes are smaller, often a converted house, with a caregiver on-site at all times. A smaller setting may appeal to your parent; ask how it handles the care and medical support they actually need. The NIA notes that group homes may not be state-inspected the way other facility types are, which makes it worth asking directly how the home is licensed, who oversees it, and what happens if a problem arises.

Nursing homes provide ongoing medical care and are state-inspected and regulated; some have a separate dementia-specific unit. These suit people whose medical needs go beyond what assisted living or a group home can provide, not just dementia symptoms on their own.

None of these is automatically “better.” The right fit depends on your parent’s current medical needs, the behaviors involved, your budget, and what’s actually available near you or near whichever family member can visit regularly.

What to ask on a tour

Before selecting a facility, ask the care team which level of care to tour. NIA’s facility-selection guidance recommends asking a health care provider about needed services and considering the person’s preferences. Bring this list, and don’t let a glossy lobby answer questions it wasn’t asked.

  • What’s the staff-to-resident ratio, during the day and overnight?
  • Can your staff safely meet my parent’s current supervision, mobility, eating and medication needs on evenings and weekends; what happens if those needs change suddenly, and who decides when this placement is no longer suitable?
  • What dementia-specific training do direct-care staff receive, and how often is it refreshed?
  • What does a typical day look like — structured activities, free time, outdoor access?
  • Is there secured or supervised outdoor space, not just an indoor common room?
  • How does the facility handle agitation, wandering attempts, or a resident who refuses care that day?
  • What’s included in the base fee, and what costs extra — incontinence supplies, medication management, transportation to appointments?
  • How is the facility licensed and inspected, and can you see the most recent inspection report?
  • What’s the process if your parent’s needs increase — does the facility handle that internally, or would another move be required?
  • How are families kept informed of day-to-day changes, falls, or medical concerns?
  • Can you visit unannounced, and can you join a meal or activity before deciding?

Bring the current care instructions, shared appropriately, and ask the person responsible for care to explain how staff would carry them out. If your parent has prescribed swallowing precautions, ask who can follow them at every meal. If transfers require trained assistance, ask who is available to provide it. Ask who administers medicine, who can contact a clinician overnight, and how an urgent change is escalated. For exit precautions, ask how supervision and safe emergency egress work together, using Chapter 13’s boundary rather than treating a secured door as the whole answer.

After each visit, date the notes and record the unanswered questions. This week, contact one search resource.

How payment questions fit in

Ask admissions for an itemized written price and which payers it accepts. Verify eligibility and what each service is covered for with Medicare or the health plan, your state Medicaid agency, or the long-term-care insurer before relying on an estimate; get professional advice before signing an unclear contract.

As Chapter 17 explained, Medicare’s long-term-care coverage page distinguishes nonmedical long-term care, which Medicare does not pay for, from potentially covered services with separate requirements. A facility’s willingness to accept a payer does not establish your parent’s eligibility. State Medicaid rules vary; check with your parent’s state agency about this setting and these services, not just the word “care.”

If GUIDE currently helps your family, tell the participating provider the precise proposed setting before relying on any continued services. CMS excludes memory-care-unit and long-term nursing-home residents; even eligible residents of partnered residential care communities cannot receive GUIDE respite. Ask what will stop and what other support is available.

The CMS GUIDE FAQ, revised September 25, 2026, states that memory-care-unit residents are ineligible as of July 2026. Approved residential-community partnerships are required beginning July 1, 2026; eligible residents may receive other GUIDE services, but not respite. Have the participating provider assess the exact placement rather than guessing from an assisted-living brochure.

Where to start looking

A few resources, named in Chapters 13 and 18 for other purposes, do double duty here. The ACL’s Eldercare Locator, or 1-800-677-1116, connects families to local aging services. Ask about the local Area Agency on Aging and help finding appropriate facilities. NIA directs readers to LongTermCare.gov at ACL for housing options and local-service information. If that page won’t load, use NIA’s linked facility guidance above or contact the Locator instead.

Medicare’s Care Compare lets you look up nursing homes, including inspection results and staffing data; it isn’t a directory of every assisted living facility or group home. Licensing and inspection for those settings vary by state. Ask your state’s licensing agency how to check the named facility’s current license and inspection history. Medicare’s staffing explanation cautions that its averages don’t show staff present at every particular moment or care given to one resident. Use the figures to ask questions, not to certify an evening shift you haven’t seen.

Ask prospective facilities about current openings and admission requirements before scheduling a visit. A place on a resource list is a lead, not confirmation that it can accept your parent or provide the needed care.

A tour that went better than expected

Here’s a made-up visit, not a Maggie-and-Dot story: a worried daughter and son tour a facility together, expecting a hard afternoon. They’d pictured something closer to a hospital hallway. Instead, a staff member kneels down to talk with a resident who’s anxious about finding her room, uses her name, and waits for an answer before moving on. The daughter notices this before she notices the furniture. Later, over coffee in the car, the siblings admit the tour reassured them more than either expected, though they’re careful to say one good interaction isn’t the whole picture. They schedule a second visit at dinnertime to see another shift and ask how many trained staff are actually on duty then.

Carry that hypothetical visit through the less reassuring part: comparing answers. The siblings have permission to share their mother’s current instructions. In this invented example, she needs supervision overnight, trained help with transfers, assistance following a prescribed swallowing plan at meals, and administered medicines. Those are her assessed needs in the example, not a list that applies to everyone with dementia. Her clinician has asked them to investigate settings able to meet those needs; the assessment isn’t a promise that any particular place can.

The first facility’s admissions representative says, “We have staff here all night.” The daughter writes that answer under overnight supervision but leaves the question open. It doesn’t say who can respond when her mother gets up or how staff cover several residents needing help together. She asks to speak with the care director. She wants an explanation of this mother’s supervision, not another description of the building’s opening hours.

At the second visit, that director explains how overnight help is assigned and identifies the trained workers available on the shift being discussed. The director says the facility would review the mother’s transfer instructions before deciding whether it could accept her. The siblings record that as an assessment still needed. They do not turn “we’ll review it” into “they can do it,” or assume today’s staff count will hold every future night.

Another facility gives a different answer: it cannot provide the assistance described in the current transfer instructions. The son likes its smaller dining room, but writes “current transfer needs not met” beside its name. That isn’t a poor score to average against the nice room. It is a specific mismatch to take back to the care team. This example doesn’t establish that all small facilities have the same limitation.

For eating, the first facility names the person who would review the prescribed swallowing plan and asks for the current instructions before confirming suitability. The siblings ask who would provide the required assistance during weekend meals. No answer yet. Under medicine administration, they record which staff the director says would administer the medicines, then ask whether that service is included in the written price. They aren’t asking staff to change the prescription or interpreting swallowing instructions themselves.

They send the dated answers and open questions to the clinician and social worker through an agreed private channel. Their question is narrow: does either setting’s described care meet the mother’s assessed needs, and what must be confirmed before choosing? The social worker asks them to obtain the first facility’s individualized care assessment and written account of what happens if needs increase. The clinician asks for clarification of the meal assistance. Neither professional has approved placement merely because a tour occurred.

One payer question is still unresolved. The long-term-care insurer hasn’t confirmed whether the mother’s policy covers this particular facility and the quoted services. The daughter labels that amount unconfirmed rather than subtracting it from the price. If GUIDE is helping now, she also asks the participating provider about the proposed memory-care unit; the CMS exclusion above cannot be treated as a benefit that continues until someone sends a bill.

The siblings have not chosen a facility by the end of the example. They have ruled out an identified mismatch and know which care and payment answers are missing. The care team helps them address current supervision while those questions are resolved. An unfinished comparison is useful when it tells you whom to call; it becomes dangerous when “still looking” is used to excuse unsafe care today.

When no option feels good.

Grief can come with you; write your parent’s specific needs, each facility’s answer, and one question for the clinician or social worker. Keep preferences beside care needs: your parent may care deeply about an outdoor place to sit or being close enough for visits. Record those wishes without letting them erase a necessary care requirement.

Use a separate line for each need, with the visit date and the name or role of whoever answered. Mark “not confirmed” where the answer depends on an assessment or a promised callback. Ask which unanswered issue prevents a safe choice; don’t give every blank the same weight. Carry the most consequential question into the next professional conversation. This comparison page is a practical aid, not a clinical score or permission to override your parent’s decision.

For the belongings, house and moving-day logistics, see Downsizing a Parent.

The conversation with your parent, if they can still have it

Depending on where your parent is in the disease, this decision may happen with them, around them, or largely without their input — and it helps to know which situation you’re actually in before you start talking. If your parent can still follow and weigh in on the conversation, include them honestly rather than presenting a move as already settled. Frame it around something concrete they care about: more help during the day, people nearby instead of alone for long stretches, a setting that can catch a fall faster than you can from another room. Avoid the word “home” as a trap — telling someone a facility is “just like home” when it plainly isn’t erodes trust fast, and dementia doesn’t erase the ability to notice a broken promise.

If your parent cannot make this particular decision, ask the care team about their decision-making ability and consult the valid documents and a licensed elder law attorney familiar with your parent’s state to establish who may decide and sign. Keep your parent involved in the ways they can participate; do not assume that being the lead caregiver grants authority.

That is the Chapter 16 authority boundary, not a new family test of capacity. The Alzheimer’s Association’s Legal Documents guidance says decision rights remain while the person has legal capacity and laws vary by state. Ask the attorney about authority for this decision and these admission papers. Include appropriately involved relatives before a decision becomes urgent, while keeping family consultation separate from the legal right to decide.

Give yourself time you may not think you have

If you can see a care gap developing, begin asking about appropriate settings before a discharge deadline forces several questions into one afternoon. You cannot forecast every change, and starting early doesn’t establish that an opening will be available.

Ask the discharge planner and care team whether an appropriate short-term setting is available and safe for your parent’s present needs; confirm its admission requirements, cost and who provides care afterward. Do not leave an unsafe discharge or supervision gap while waiting.

Use NIA’s linked long-term-care guidance to support that conversation, not as proof that a short stay exists nearby. Tell the discharge team plainly what care cannot be provided at home. Leave the next conversation with the name of the person following up on that gap, not just a brochure on the passenger seat.

A Little More Room to Live

With Mama’s hymn over tea still in my ears, I want to leave you without pretending the work is finished.

Mama’s opinions about music were hers; my reading of an expression was not a decision.

You may have arrived at this page with several matters still open. Reading to the end hasn’t closed them. The work you’ve already done stands beside those unanswered questions.

The title says first year because a book needs a boundary. A family doesn’t receive one with the diagnosis. The worry may have started earlier; the name for it may arrive later. A month can hold both familiar habits and a new care question, sometimes before anybody has found words for the change. The calendar keeps its own pace regardless. I use livable for the part that can’t be measured by a date or a finished answer. It doesn’t promise that a difficult thing will become easy, or that the next year will follow this one. It is a modest word for a stretch of time that still contains ordinary days.

You cleared a walking route and checked the light by the chair. Some evenings still went badly. Nobody else may have seen the work you did before they arrived.

The current-care boundary in Chapter 19 still stands: help needed now comes before an ordinary planning task or another page of reading.

Chapter 18’s safe-coverage condition still matters. Once someone suitable has taken the shift, the hour belongs to you. You may sit through it without coming back with a better plan.

For the ordinary planning work, choose one unfinished item from a checklist you already used in this book. One actual task that still matters to your family. Give it an owner who has accepted it and a drop date, and put that agreement beside the item. The task may be yours. It needn’t be.

Leave the book open at that line.
